recent_posts.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
recent_posts.text: Phone return scams are part of a very convincing social engineering method where the criminals get a phone and you get billed. A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out. Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay. Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments. How phone return scams work The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns: “After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.” Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. recent_posts.title: Technology that blocks DGA domains | Kaspersky official blog
recent_posts.text: Kaspersky email security solutions now include a technology that detects domains with auto-generated names. We use many technologies to detect email spam. They analyze every part of a message: headers, text, images, and links. But the first thing our email products focus on is the “From” field. If the address contains a domain that’s already on our denylist, it’s an easy call. But spammers know the drill, so they register domains in industrial quantities to make emails, even from a single campaign, arrive from completely different addresses. Clearly, they don’t do that by hand. The process has long been automated, and attackers’ algorithms can register huge numbers of domains in a matter of minutes. But every domain needs a name. Coming up with a unique one for each isn’t feasible. So spammers use domain generation algorithms (DGAs), which create similar names with minor variations, based on date and time, pseudo-random numbers, and so on. In fact, to block mailings such as these, you don’t need every address on your denylist. We’re good at automating processes, too. recent_posts.title: Five Findings From the 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
recent_posts.text: What 768 security professionals told us about consolidation, ROI, and AI. Get five takeaways from the 2027 State of Threat Intelligence. The much anticipated State of Threat Intelligence report has just been published. The State of Threat Intelligence report is based on a survey Recorded Future conducted with UserEvidence of 768 cybersecurity professionals at enterprises with at least 1,000 employees. It’s the latest edition in our annual report series, where we gauge how threat intelligence is currently being used, funded, and measured. When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program and is planning for the year ahead. Here are my top five findings and why. 1. Cost is the least common reason to consolidate A strong majority of respondents (79%) said they plan to consolidate threat intelligence vendors in the next year. That alone is no huge surprise, especially given that respondents reported using an average of five different vendors. recent_posts.title: Google says Russian-speaking hackers ran the first fully automated AI cyberattack
recent_posts.text: Google's Threat Intelligence Group says the tools trade stealth for speed, leaving noisy forensic traces even as they succeed on their own. The post Google says Russian-speaking hackers ran the first fully automated AI cyberattack appeared first on CyberScoop . Google said Monday that Russian-speaking hackers carried out what its analysts believe is the first cyberattack run end-to-end by artificial intelligence, without a human in the loop at any stage of the intrusion. The operation appears in a quarterly report from Google’s Threat Intelligence Group and its Mandiant incident response unit. Researchers stopped short of naming a group or state. Their attribution rests on Russian-language comments in the operation’s code, including a configuration file instructing its user to enter API keys for “auto-exploitation” there rather than in a chat. recent_posts.title: How to prepare your digital accounts for after your death
recent_posts.text: Make it easier for loved ones to manage your online accounts, preserve important files, and follow your wishes. A little preparation can make your digital life easier for loved ones to manage after your death. Here’s how to record your wishes, protect your privacy, and give the right people a way to act. Start with a digital inventory Your next of kin cannot manage accounts they do not know exist. Create an inventory of the important parts of your digital life, including: Primary and recovery email addresses Phones, computers, tablets, and the mobile carrier associated with them Cloud storage, photo services, and backups Social media, messaging, and professional networking accounts Your password manager and its emergency-access arrangements Online banking, payment, shopping, subscription, and utility accounts Domains, websites, digital businesses, and developer accounts Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets, and the location of securely stored recovery materials For each service, include the account email or username and a profile link or account reference where relevant. recent_posts.text: Imagine buying a brand new hardware wallet for your cryptocurrency with the shrink-wrap still on... what could possibly be hiding inside? We break out a Geiger counter and a cat to find out. Meanwhile, malicious ads are targeting journalists with zero-click attacks. Plus, Origin’s Spencer Thompson reveals what AI agents are really getting up to on your employees’ laptops when nobody’s looking.
